front: In the abstract, how does Sprite achieve high performance?
back: It uses large main-memory disk block caches, with non-write-through caching on both client and server machines.

front: The paper gives two distinct advantages of caching. What are they?
back: It reduces delays (a cached block is returned much faster than one fetched from disk) and reduces contention for the disk arm when several processes access files on the same disk.

front: How much faster does the introduction say a cached block is returned versus one fetched from disk?
back: Five to ten times more quickly.

front: What did prior timesharing measurements show about cache size, per the introduction?
back: Even small caches give substantial benefits, and the benefit grows as physical memories grow [LEFF84, OUST85].

front: In Figure 1's data-flow model, where is a file access presented first, and where does a miss go?
back: A file access goes first to the local workstation's cache (file traffic); a miss goes either to the local disk if the file is stored there (disk traffic) or to the server where the file is stored (server traffic). Servers maintain their own caches to reduce disk traffic.

front: How do the benefits of a cache differ between a machine with a disk and a client, per Section 1?
back: On a machine with a disk the cache reduces disk delay and contention; on a client it additionally reduces communication delay, network contention, and server-machine contention.

front: What scalability argument from the literature does Section 1 cite for client caching?
back: Server CPUs appear to be the bottleneck in several existing network file systems [SATY85, LAZO86], so client caching offers greater system scalability as well as increased performance.

front: What two "unusual aspects" does the paper name for Sprite?
back: (1) A consistency guarantee even under simultaneous multi-client access, giving exactly the same semantics as all processes running on a single timesharing system; (2) caches that vary in size dynamically.

front: What averaged speedup did client caching give diskless workstations, per Section 1?
back: A speedup of about 10-40% for programs on diskless workstations relative to diskless workstations without client caches.

text: With client caching, server utilization dropped from about {{c1::5-18%}} per active client to about {{c2::1-9%}}, and the paper infers a single server should support at least {{c3::50}} clients.
extra: These are the introduction's figures (Section 1). Section 7.2.2 (Figure 3) reports the same measurement as about 5-20% without client caching and 2-9% with it.

front: How did Sprite compare to NFS and Andrew on a file-intensive benchmark, per the introduction?
back: Sprite completed it 30-35% faster than NFS and Andrew; Sprite's server utilization was substantially less than NFS but more than Andrew.

front: What project was Sprite built as part of, and on what hardware did the preliminary version run?
back: Sprite was built at Berkeley as part of SPUR, a high-performance multiprocessor workstation [HILL86]; the preliminary version ran on Sun-2 and Sun-3 workstations with about 1-2 MIPS and 4-16 MB of memory.

front: What were Sprite's design-target assumptions about future machines and disks?
back: Five to ten times the processing power and memory plus small degrees of multiprocessing; networks of up to a few hundred workstations; and most workstations with no local disk, with large fast disks concentrated on a few servers (diskless-by-design).

front: What interface does Sprite present to users?
back: A UNIX-like interface [RITC74]: a single shared file hierarchy accessible equally from any workstation, name space managed as in [WELCH86a], and UNIX-like open/close/read/write system calls.

front: What communication facility is the Sprite kernel built around, and how does it relate to Birrell & Nelson?
back: The kernel was completely re-implemented for network integration around a kernel-to-kernel RPC facility [WELCH86b] using a protocol similar to Birrell & Nelson [BIRR84]; the file system uses RPC extensively for cache management. The RPC is a dependency, not the paper's subject.

front: What was the primary motivation for Sprite's cache design, and what did it show?
back: The BSD study [OUST85], a trace-driven analysis of file activity on several time-shared UNIX 4.2 BSD systems, which showed even small file caches cut disk traffic and large caches (4-16 MB) cut it by as much as 90%.
source: Section 3: Background Work (the BSD study and server-contention motivation)

front: What forward-looking inference did the BSD study draw about memory and disks?
back: Increasing memory sizes will soon make it possible to keep entire file working sets in main memory, with disks serving primarily as backup.
source: Section 3: Background Work (the BSD study and server-contention motivation)

front: What hypothesis-and-caveat did the authors state about the BSD study?
back: The BSD study was on timesharing machines, not networks of workstations, so the authors hypothesized the results would carry to a network and that remote-access overhead could be cut by caching on clients as well as servers; Sections 5.3 and 7 provide the supporting simulation and measurement data.
source: Section 3: Background Work (the BSD study and server-contention motivation)

front: What two independent sources support the server-contention motivation in Section 3?
back: Lazowska et al. concluded the server CPU is the primary scalability bottleneck [LAZO86], and the Andrew designers independently redesigned their system to offload servers [SATY85] with substantial gains [HOWA87].
source: Section 3: Background Work (the BSD study and server-contention motivation)

front: What three explicit questions frame Section 4 (Basic Cache Design)?
back: Where client caches should live (memory vs local disk), how caches should be structured and addressed, and what the write-back policy should be. Consistency and sizing are deferred to Sections 5 and 6.

front: Where did prior network file systems keep client caches, and what did Sprite choose?
back: Andrew [SATY85, HOWA87] and Cedar [SCHR85] kept client caches on local disk; Sprite chose main memory.
source: 4.1 Caches on Disk or in Main Memory?

front: What four reasons did Sprite give for putting client caches in main memory?
back: (1) It permits diskless, cheaper, quieter workstations; (2) data is accessed faster from memory than a disk cache; (3) client memories are now large enough for high hit ratios; (4) server caches are in memory anyway, so memory on clients too meant one caching mechanism for both.
source: 4.1 Caches on Disk or in Main Memory?

text: Sprite reports that a {{c1::1-MB}} client cache gives greater than {{c2::80%}} read hits.
extra: One of the four reasons for choosing main-memory client caches.
source: 4.1 Caches on Disk or in Main Memory?

text: Sprite caches are organized on a block basis with a fixed {{c1::4-KB}} block size, chosen largely for simplicity and explicitly provisional.

front: How are Sprite cache blocks addressed, and why?
back: Virtually, by a unique file identifier (from the server) plus a block number within the file. Virtual addresses let a client create new blocks in its cache without first contacting a server for their physical location, and let blocks be found without traversing the file's disk map.

front: What does a client cache versus what a server additionally caches?
back: A client caches only data blocks for remote files; servers additionally cache file maps and other disk-management information, addressed by physical disk address plus a special device file identifier.

front: What two advantages does delayed write-back have over write-through?
back: Writes complete quickly because they hit the cache, and data deleted before write-back need never be written at all. The reliability cost is that unwritten data is lost on a crash.

front: Why does the paper reject write-on-close (used by Andrew and NFS)?
back: The BSD open-duration data (75% of files open <0.5 s, 90% <10 s) means write-on-close would not significantly cut traffic; it also forces the closing process to wait for the write-through, undercutting the benefit of delayed writes.

front: What consistency guarantees do NFS and Andrew provide, per Section 5?
back: Once a file is closed all data is on the server and future opens by other clients pick up the new version; under sequential write-sharing each client always sees the up-to-date version; but under concurrent write-sharing the others do not see changes immediately, and users are warned off it.

front: How does Section 5 define sequential vs concurrent write-sharing (NFS/Andrew baseline)?
back: Sequential write-sharing: a file is shared but never open for read and write on different clients at once. Concurrent write-sharing: a file is open simultaneously on several clients with at least one modifying.

front: What consistency guarantee does Sprite make, and how does it differ from NFS/Andrew?
back: Sprite permits both concurrent and sequential write-sharing and guarantees that any read returns the most recently written data regardless of when or where it was written.

front: What motivates Sprite's strong consistency, and what case is the algorithm optimized for?
back: A clean user model and encouraging the file system as a shared system-wide store (print spoolers, mailers). Since concurrent sharing is expected to be infrequent, the algorithm is optimized for the no-sharing case.

front: What is the consistency-vs-synchronization distinction the paper draws?
back: Sprite provides consistency (each read returns the most up-to-date data) but not correct synchronization; it cannot ensure concurrent applications order their reads and writes sensibly. If order matters, applications must use file-locking calls or other communication. Consistency simply reduces the problem to what it was on timesharing systems.

front: What role does the server play as the control point for consistency?
back: Each server guarantees consistency for files on its disks, clients deal only with the server (no client-client interaction), and the algorithm depends on the server being notified on every open and close so it can detect imminent concurrent write-sharing. This prohibits name caching.

front: How does Sprite define a concurrently write-shared file, and what does it do?
back: A file is concurrently write-shared when it is open on multiple clients and at least one has it open for writing. Sprite disables client caching for such a file; all reads and writes go to the server.

front: What are Sprite's scoping rules for disabling caching under concurrent write-sharing?
back: Disabling is per file and only while concurrent write-sharing holds; a file can be cached by many clients as long as none writes, and a single writer may cache it with no concurrent readers or writers elsewhere. Only currently-open clients are notified; clients holding stale blocks act at their next open.

front: How does Section 5.2 define sequential write-sharing?
back: A file modified by one client, closed, then opened by another. The paper identifies two separate problems with two separate mechanisms.

front: What is sequential-write-sharing problem one, and how does Sprite solve it?
back: Stale blocks in the opener's own cache, solved by version numbers: the server keeps a per-file version number and increments it each time the file is opened for writing; each client stores the version of every file it caches and, on open, compares against the server's version and flushes its copy if they differ. Similar to NFS and early Andrew.

front: What trace and simulation methodology produced the Section 5.3 results?
back: The BSD trace (3-day mid-week intervals on three VAX-11/780s running 4.2 BSD for program development, text processing, and CAD [OUST85]) was fed to a simulator that treated each timesharing user as a separate client workstation in a network with one file server. The paper uses the trace for Sprite here and again in the Section 7 server-sizing estimate.

front: In Table 1, how does the server-traffic ratio fall as client cache grows from 0.5 MB to 8 MB?
back: A 0.5-MB client cache drops the ratio to 32%, 1 MB to 29%, 2 MB to 28%, and it is essentially flat (28%) at 4 and 8 MB. So client caching cut server traffic by over 70% and gave read hit ratios over 80%.

front: What does Table 2 (consistency ignored) show, and what does comparing it to Table 1 reveal?
back: The same simulation with no attempt to guarantee consistency drops the 0.5-MB ratio to 28% and the 8-MB ratio to 21%. Comparing bottom-right entries shows about one-fourth of all server traffic in Table 1 is due to cache consistency. Table 2 is not realistic (incorrect results) but gives an upper bound on what a cleverer consistency mechanism could save.

front: What goal motivates Section 6 (Virtual Memory and the File System)?
back: Let each client cache be as large as possible (an application with small VM needs should use most of physical memory as file cache), unlike UNIX's fixed-size caches. Sprite lets each file cache grow and shrink dynamically by having the file system and virtual memory modules negotiate over physical memory.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: How do the VM and file-system modules keep their pages ordered, and how do they negotiate memory?
back: VM keeps pages in approximate LRU order via a clock algorithm [NELS86]; the file system keeps blocks in perfect LRU order because all accesses go through read/write. Each records a time-of-last-access. When either needs memory, it compares the age of its oldest page with the other's; if the other owns the older page it is forced to give it up, otherwise the module recycles its own oldest page.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: What is the double-caching problem in Section 6, and how is it fixed?
back: VM is itself a file-system user (backing storage is ordinary files; read-only code is demand-loaded from executables), so pages could land in both caches or move into the file cache to age again. Fix: VM bypasses the local file cache for backing files; for demand-loaded code already in the file cache, the page is copied to the VM pool and the file-cache block is given an infinite age so it is replaced first.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: Even though VM bypasses the local file cache for backing files, where are those files still cached?
back: On servers, which makes servers' memories into an extended main memory for their clients.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: What is the multi-block-pages problem in Section 6, and Sprite's simple solution?
back: When a VM page holds several file blocks (Sun-3 has 8-KB pages but 4-KB blocks), what is the page's LRU age and what happens to the other blocks when it is relinquished? Sprite's solution: a page's age is the age of its youngest block, and when a page is relinquished all its blocks are removed. The authors are still investigating this policy.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: What two centralized alternatives did the authors consider and reject in Section 6?
back: (1) Access everything through VM by memory-mapping files, as in Apollo's DOMAIN [LEACH83]; rejected mainly because a mapped-file approach must cache a file's pages before access, so consistency could not be implemented by refusing to cache shared files. (2) A centralized physical-memory manager for both subsystems; rejected because the logical way to compute page ages differs between VM and files, and the distributed scheme shares only page age and LRU while letting each module age pages its own way and even adjust relative aging rates.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: What initial-experience tuning note does Section 6 give about VM vs file pages?
back: VM pages should get preferential treatment under memory contention, because the sequential nature of file access means a low file hit ratio hurts far less than a low VM hit ratio.
source: Section 6: Virtual Memory and the File System

front: What five measurement questions do the Section 7 benchmarks target?
back: How much faster file-intensive programs run with client caches; how much client caches cut server CPU load; how much they cut network load; how many clients a server/network can support; and how the benefits scale with CPU speed and memory.

front: What was the Section 7 measurement configuration?
back: Sun-3 workstations (~2 MIPS); clients were Sun-3/75 and Sun-3/160 with at least 8 MB; the server was a Sun-3/180 with 12 MB and a 400-MB Fujitsu Eagle disk.

front: In Table 3, what were the local-disk vs diskless elapsed times (and server CPU) for Open/Close?
back: Open/Close: 2.17 ms local disk vs 8.11 ms diskless elapsed, 3.75 ms of it server CPU.

front: In Table 3, what were the times for Failed Open and Get Attributes (stat)?
back: Failed Open: 1.48 ms local vs 4.13 ms diskless (2.01 ms server). Get Attributes (stat): 1.28 ms vs 4.47 ms (2.12 ms server).

front: What two general findings did Table 3 (name-lookup micro-benchmarks) show?
back: Remote versions took 3-4 times as long as local operations, and about half the remote elapsed time was spent in the server CPU.

text: In Table 4, sequential read throughput (KB/s) was {{c1::3269}} local cache, {{c2::475}} server cache, {{c3::224}} local disk, {{c4::212}} server disk.
extra: Accesses were rigged to be satisfied in one place.

text: In Table 4, sequential write throughput (KB/s) was {{c1::2893}} local cache, {{c2::380}} server cache, {{c3::197}} local disk, {{c4::176}} server disk.

front: What two results does the paper draw from Table 4?
back: A client reads its own cache 6-8 times faster than the server's cache, so client caching could in the best case make a program run 6-8x faster; and a client reads/writes the server cache at about local-disk speed.

front: Why is the server cache about 2x faster than local disk in Table 4, and what do the authors expect?
back: The current 2x server-cache advantage is an artifact of Sprite's disk layout (one block per disk revolution); they expect eventually to reach 4.3 BSD disk throughput (2-3x the Table 4 rates), after which local disk and server cache would be comparable. As CPUs outpace disks, the server cache should beat local disk up to network-bandwidth limits, so a large server cache may beat a local disk even for paging.

front: What was the Section 7.2 macro-benchmark methodology?
back: Well-known UNIX programs ported to Sprite, each run three times per data point and averaged. Table 5 lists six benchmarks (Andrew, Fs-make, Simulator, Sort, Diff, Nroff) with their I/O intensity (KB/s read, write).

front: What is the Andrew benchmark (Table 5), and its I/O intensity?
back: Copy a 70-file/200-KB directory tree, stat every file, read every byte, compile and link (Satyanarayanan's Andrew benchmark [HOWA87]); 54.9 KB/s read, 34.4 KB/s write.

front: What are the Fs-make and Simulator benchmarks (Table 5)?
back: Fs-make: recompile the Sprite file system (33 files/33,800 lines of C), 56.6/28.9 KB/s. Simulator: set-associative cache simulation from a 3375-KB address trace, 23.0/0.0 KB/s.

front: What are the Sort, Diff, and Nroff benchmarks (Table 5) and their I/O intensity?
back: Sort: sort a 1-MB file, 47.0/90.2 KB/s. Diff: compare two identical 1-MB files, 252.4/0 KB/s. Nroff: format the paper itself, 16.1/18.1 KB/s.

front: How does Table 6 structure its measurements, and what is the worst-case warm client-caching result?
back: Table 6 gives per-benchmark elapsed times across three configurations (local disk; diskless with server cache only; diskless with client and server caches), each cold and warm, normalized to warm local-disk time. Without client caching diskless machines were generally about 10-50% slower; with client caching and a warm start the gap was in the worst case only about 12%.

front: Why do the authors expect the client-caching advantage to grow over time (Section 7.2.1)?
back: Larger memories make larger (more effective) caches feasible, and processors are getting faster faster than networks or disks, so uncached workstations will increasingly wait on network/disk.

front: How much did client caching cut server CPU load, per Figure 3 (Section 7.2.2)?
back: A diskless client without a client cache used about 5-20% of the server CPU; with client caching this dropped to 2-9%. The figure caption states the reduction as a factor of 2-5.

front: What network utilization did the benchmarks show without client caching (Section 7.2.3)?
back: Without client caching the benchmarks averaged 6.5% utilization of the 10-Mbit/s Ethernet, with diff alone using 15% for a single client. A machine five times faster than a Sun-3 (SPUR or the Sun-4) would use 30-50% of the Ethernet running the benchmarks uncached.

front: How much did client caching cut network utilization, and what does that imply (Section 7.2.3)?
back: Client caching cut network utilization by about a factor of four, to an average of about 1.5%, which the authors judge enough to keep 10-Mbit Ethernet adequate for one or two more CPU generations.

front: How was the Section 7.2.4 multi-client contention experiment set up?
back: Several copies of Andrew (the most server-intensive benchmark) were run on different clients, each on its own copy of input/output files, so there was no cache-consistency overhead. Figure 4 shows the effect on client speed, server CPU, and network.

front: With seven clients, how did performance differ with and without client caching (Figure 4)?
back: With seven clients and no client caching, clients ran two-and-a-half times slower, the server was nearly 80% utilized, and the network over 30% utilized. With client caching and seven clients, each ran within 30% of local-disk speed, server utilization about 50%, network only 5%.

front: How does the paper derive that one Sprite server should support at least 50 users (Section 7.2.4)?
back: Figure 4 suggests one Sun-3 server supports at least ten Sun-3 clients running Andrew simultaneously, and one Andrew instance is estimated to equal about 5-20 active users, so a server should support at least 50 users.

front: What is the basis of the paper's estimate that one Andrew-benchmark instance equals about 5-20 active users?
back: The BSD study's .5-1.8 KB/s per active user, scaled up 8-10x (to 4-18 KB/s) for paging traffic and faster machines, compared against Andrew's 90 KB/s average.

front: Against what two external figures do the authors cross-check the 5-20 users-per-Andrew estimate?
back: Howard et al.'s estimate that one Andrew instance is about five average users [HOWA87], and Lazowska et al.'s figure of about 4 KB/s per user [LAZO86].

front: How should Sprite server capacity change as CPU speeds rise, per Section 7.2.4?
back: It should not change much as long as client and server CPU speeds grow at about the same rate, and it should be even higher when servers are more powerful than clients.

front: What does Table 7 compare, and on which five parameters?
back: It compares Sprite with six systems (NFS, RFS, Andrew, Locus, Apollo, Cedar/CFS) on cache location, cache size, writing policy, consistency guarantees, and cache validation.

front: In Table 7, how is Sprite characterized across the five parameters?
back: Memory; variable size; 30-s delay writing policy; sequential+concurrent consistency; ask-server-on-open validation.

front: In Table 7, how are NFS and Andrew characterized?
back: NFS: memory, fixed, on-close or 30-s delay, sequential, ask-server-on-open. Andrew: disk, fixed, on-close, sequential, server-calls-client-when-modified.

front: In Table 7, how is RFS characterized?
back: Memory; fixed size; write-through; sequential+concurrent consistency; ask-server-on-open validation.

front: In Table 7, how is Locus characterized?
back: Memory; fixed size; on-close writing; sequential+concurrent consistency; ask-server-on-open validation.

front: In Table 7, how is Apollo characterized?
back: Memory; variable size; delayed or on-unlock writing; sequential consistency; validation by asking the server on lock. Apollo uses lock/unlock rather than open/close.

front: In Table 7, how is CFS/Cedar characterized?
back: Disk; variable size; writing on SModel (a tool for moving changed cached files back to the server); consistency guarantees and validation both "not applicable". CFS caches only immutable files.

front: Besides Sprite, which systems support both sequential and concurrent write-sharing, and how do they differ?
back: Only RFS and Locus. RFS handles concurrent sharing like Sprite (disable caching) but is write-through and disables caching on the first write rather than at open. Locus supports concurrent write-sharing without disabling caching, using a read/write token-passing scheme where kernels pass tokens and flush caches.

front: Apollo does not support concurrent write-sharing. What does it offer instead, per Section 8?
back: Lock/unlock primitives that readers and writers can use to serialize their accesses, with cache flushing that is correct if the primitives are used correctly.

front: How does Andrew's cache validation differ from the other systems, per Section 8?
back: Every Table 7 system except Andrew checks with the server on open or lock to validate the cached copy. Andrew began with check-on-open but was redesigned so servers track which clients cache which files and notify (call back) clients when a file is modified, letting clients open cached files without contacting the server. Sprite deliberately processes all opens and naming on the server to avoid client name-cache complexity.

front: What does Table 8 estimate, and how?
back: The upper bound if Sprite added name caching + callback, estimated by counting Open and Get-Attributes invocations and assuming all could be done on the client with no network/server involvement.

front: What are the Table 8 estimated improvements for the Andrew benchmark with name caching + callback?
back: Andrew benchmark degradation 12.5% to 6.2%, server utilization 8.9% to 5.6%, network utilization 1.04% to 0.69%.

front: What are the Table 8 estimated improvements for Fs-make, and the overall conclusion?
back: Fs-make degradation 5.6% to 1.0%, server 6.7% to 4.1%, network 0.75% to 0.45%. Conclusion: client-visible performance would improve only a few percent, but server and network utilization would fall by as much as one-third, potentially letting one server or network support 50% more clients.

front: Why is Sprite's estimated callback gain smaller than Andrew's measured gain?
back: The authors attribute it to Andrew's servers being user-level processes (more portable, but remote operations much more expensive than in Sprite's kernel-level implementation); had Andrew's servers been in the kernel, there would have been less motivation to switch to callback.

front: What does Figure 5 compare, and how were the numbers normalized?
back: Andrew-benchmark running time and server CPU utilization vs number of clients, for Sprite, Andrew, and NFS. NFS/Andrew numbers come from [HOWA87] on Sun-3/50 clients; Sprite was measured on Sun-3/75s (about 30% faster) and renormalized for Sun-3/50 (elapsed times multiplied by 1.3, server utilization divided by 1.3). Sprite accessed binaries, paging, and temp files remotely whereas NFS/Andrew used local disks for them.

front: For a single client, how much faster was Sprite than NFS and Andrew on the Andrew benchmark, and why (Section 8)?
back: About 30% faster than NFS and about 35% faster than Andrew, credited to Sprite's fast kernel-to-kernel RPC, delayed writes, and kernel (vs Andrew's user-level) implementation.

front: As clients increased in Figure 5, how much server CPU per client did Andrew, Sprite, and NFS use?
back: Andrew about 2.4%, Sprite 5.4%, NFS over 20%. NFS saturated quickly; Andrew scaled best, an advantage the authors attribute to callbacks.

front: How does Section 8 restate the claim that a Sprite server should support at least 50 clients?
back: NFS supports 10-20 clients per server, and Sprite's server utilization is one-fourth of NFS's.

front: What two unresolved issues does Section 9 (Future Work) name?
back: Crash recovery and disk overflow.

front: Why is Sprite fragile on a crash, and how does NFS differ?
back: Sprite keeps state in each server's main memory; a server crash loses dirty cache blocks and open-file information, so client processes using that server's files usually have to be killed. NFS servers are stateless, which is less efficient (everything written through to disk) but lets clients sleep through a server crash and continue after reboot with no ill effects.

front: What recovery direction does Section 9 propose, and what makes it cheap?
back: Make server caches write-through (client caches stay delayed-write), since even the most intensive benchmark generated server data at under 20 KB/s while a client can write a server disk at 176 KB/s (Table 4), so write-through at the server may cost little. Combined with clients supplying enough information to re-open files after a crash, this aims for transparent continuation.

front: What is the disk-overflow problem in Section 9, and the planned fix?
back: A client does not tell the server when it allocates new blocks, so a block written up to 30 s later may find no disk space, unlike UNIX where write reports a full disk immediately. The planned fix is a quota system: each client gets a block quota and requests more when it runs out; when free space is too low for quotas, clients must send explicit allocation requests on every new block.

front: What does the paper's conclusion say Sprite demonstrates?
back: Large caches give high-performance access to shared files; large client caches let diskless workstations match disk-equipped ones while using only a small share of server CPU; consistency is cheap because write-sharing is rare; dynamic cache sizing keeps file caches as large as possible without hurting VM.

front: What buyer's-advice line does the conclusion give about local disks vs memory?
back: For anyone considering a local disk, spend the same amount of money on additional memory instead, because more memory helps both file-system performance (larger cache) and virtual-memory performance, more than a local disk would.

front: The lecture presents the two-thirds figure as a count of improvable operations. How does Nelson et al. actually frame it?
back: As a ceiling: because about 1/3 of accesses are writes, write-through cannot reduce disk or server traffic by more than two-thirds. The arithmetic is the same, but the paper's phrasing is an upper bound on savings, not a tally of operations. (Write-through itself is reliable but makes each write wait for the disk.)
